prompt:
A response network must choose one dispatch bundle for an east-lane hazmat scare. Root-level evidence strongly favors a fatal wait-or-open-corridor mistake unless a specific pair of deep-leaf facts climbs all the way to the root. Choose the single bundle consistent with all observations together.
A: hold the hazmat team centrally and keep the corridor open until direct visual confirmation arrives
B: send the hazmat team east now but keep the corridor open because the event is still local
C: send the hazmat team east now, restrict the main corridor, and verify the north alarm remotely
D: send the hazmat team north first because the degraded corridor alarm may still represent a passenger risk
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: By dispatch protocol, repeated east heat pings without both hazardous inventory and corridor-exposure risk are not enough to justify corridor restriction. With only root evidence, A looks safest.
agent_observations.agent_1: The north camera heater failed, so the north alarm alone should not pull the only hazmat team away. That weakens D but still leaves A and B looking reasonable.
agent_observations.agent_2: Remote verification for the north corridor can launch in minutes, so a north-first dispatch is unnecessary, but that still does not prove the east corridor must be closed.
agent_observations.agent_3: If both hazardous inventory and corridor-exposure risk are confirmed, the book requires immediate corridor restriction and east dispatch. Missing either one means do not close the corridor.
agent_observations.agent_4: Yesterday's shift log says the east storage lane looked clear after cleanup, which superficially supports waiting and makes B or A feel more plausible.
agent_observations.agent_5: The thermal pings all come from the same bay sensor cluster, so root-level operators may dismiss them as a local false concentration rather than a corridor threat.
agent_observations.agent_6: The corridor is expensive to close operationally, so without a hard trigger the safer-looking local choice remains A.
agent_observations.agent_7: The deep inventory manifest confirms a solvent pallet is still staged in the exact east bay that is producing the repeated heat pings. This is one of the two facts root is missing.
agent_observations.agent_8: Current wind direction will push vapor from that east bay into the main corridor within minutes if the bay event is real. This is the second fact needed to overturn the root's open-corridor bias.

prompt:
A parcel network lost one hub and must pick one routing bundle. Root dashboards make unrestricted rebalancing look safe unless two deep-leaf constraints propagate upward. Choose the single bundle consistent with all observations together.
A: rebalance across two healthy hubs with queue caps and low-priority throttling; route nothing through the failed hub
B: rebalance across two healthy hubs without queue caps; keep all admission rates normal because both dashboards still show spare capacity
C: route premium traffic through the failed hub's cached forwarders while flooding the smallest healthy hub with the rest of the overflow
D: stop all parcels nationally until the failed hub recovers so downstream hubs stay perfectly balanced
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: Top-level capacity dashboards still show spare throughput at the two healthy hubs, so B looks attractive if no deeper constraint is known.
agent_observations.agent_1: Premium SLA pressure makes low-priority throttling feel operationally painful, so root operators lean against A unless it is strictly necessary.
agent_observations.agent_2: A national stop is obviously too broad, but that still leaves B looking like the least disruptive path.
agent_observations.agent_3: If either queue caps or low-priority throttling is actually required, then B fails even though the current dashboard snapshot looks comfortable.
agent_observations.agent_4: The smallest healthy hub is not the bottleneck shown on the executive dashboard, so operators may underestimate how quickly it saturates under redirected load.
agent_observations.agent_5: The failed hub has not fully disappeared from some stale views, which can keep C superficially alive even though it is dangerous.
agent_observations.agent_6: Premium traffic alone is not enough to expose the coming queue cliff; the dangerous effect appears only after several waves of normal-priority load.
agent_observations.agent_7: A deeper capacity model shows one healthy hub crosses its queue cliff within the hour unless explicit queue caps are applied. This is one of the two hidden facts root lacks.
agent_observations.agent_8: Another deep planning run shows premium SLA is preserved only if low-priority traffic is throttled after the caps are applied. Queue caps alone are insufficient. This is the second hidden fact that turns B into a fatal choice.

prompt:
A coordination team must choose one failover bundle after sustained packet loss on a single inter-region path. The root controller strongly prefers an immediate cutover unless deep-leaf constraints propagate through the tree. Choose the single bundle consistent with all observations together.
A: drain traffic gradually to the healthy region, keep retries enabled, and use the tested rollback threshold during the drain
B: cut traffic over immediately to the healthy region, keep retries enabled, and treat rollback as optional because the healthy region looks stable
C: drain traffic gradually but disable retries globally to reduce chatter during the move
D: hold traffic on the degraded region a bit longer and gather more telemetry before doing anything disruptive
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: The top-level healthy-region dashboard shows visible spare headroom, so an immediate cutover looks like the fastest and safest response. Root therefore leans toward B.
agent_observations.agent_1: Rollback machinery exists, but if the healthy region were truly comfortable, operators might reasonably treat rollback as secondary rather than central.
agent_observations.agent_2: Holding traffic on the degraded region is dangerous because the loss has persisted too long, so D is weak, but B still looks plausible from root's point of view.
agent_observations.agent_3: If either the healthy-region headroom is less robust than it looks or retries remain important, then B is no longer safe and the slower drain becomes necessary.
agent_observations.agent_4: Current alert summaries aggregate several pools together, which can hide a local queue cliff even when the global dashboard looks fine.
agent_observations.agent_5: Transient self-heal windows have passed, so waiting longer will not magically fix the path, but that alone does not disprove B.
agent_observations.agent_6: Disabling retries globally would recover some bandwidth but could silently discard work if retries are still paying off.
agent_observations.agent_7: A deep queue model shows the healthy region can absorb a staged drain but not an instant full cutover spike; immediate cutover will brush its own queue threshold. This is one hidden fact root is missing.
agent_observations.agent_8: A deeper transaction audit shows retries are still rescuing a meaningful share of requests, so disabling them globally would throw away recoverable work. This is the second hidden fact that makes only A viable.

prompt:
A coastal logistics mesh must choose one congestion-response bundle. Root dispatch sees spare inland space and a collapsing port road, so a blunt divert-everything policy looks locally correct unless deep-leaf facts propagate upward. Choose the single bundle consistent with all observations together.
A: divert every incoming load inland, including reefer cargo, and keep the port nearly idle until congestion clears
B: divert non-perishable loads inland, keep timed reefer slots at the port, and meter access-road recovery instead of flooding the queue
C: keep routing all loads to the port but slow dispatch slightly and hope crane throughput catches up
D: stop national shipping for the day so the port road stays uncongested everywhere
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: The access road is close to gridlock while inland depots still show visible spare buffer, so a blanket inland diversion makes immediate local sense. Root therefore leans toward A.
agent_observations.agent_1: Keeping all traffic aimed at the port is clearly too risky, so C is weak, but that still leaves A as the apparently prudent response.
agent_observations.agent_2: A national stop is broader than the observed congestion zone, but without deeper cold-chain detail A still appears attractive.
agent_observations.agent_3: If inland depots cannot absorb every cargo class, then blanket diversion fails and the response must become selective instead.
agent_observations.agent_4: Executive inland-capacity views do not break out refrigerated versus non-refrigerated storage, so they overstate how much cargo can actually be diverted.
agent_observations.agent_5: The port can still process some scheduled cold-chain loads, but that fact does not appear on the root dispatch dashboard.
agent_observations.agent_6: Metered recovery only works if non-perishable inflow is peeled away first, otherwise the access road never falls back below the congestion threshold.
agent_observations.agent_7: Deep depot inventory shows inland sites do not have enough refrigerated capacity to absorb all reefer loads. This hidden fact makes blanket diversion A fail.
agent_observations.agent_8: A deeper terminal schedule shows timed reefer slots can still be processed safely at the port if non-perishables are diverted and road recovery is metered. This second hidden fact turns B into the only viable plan.

prompt:
An emergency communications mesh lost one relay tower during a storm. Choose the best traffic policy.
A: broadcast everything on every channel to maximize reach
B: shut down remaining towers to protect hardware from overload
C: keep routing through the failed relay in case it recovers
D: reweight the mesh to surviving towers and reserve bandwidth for urgent traffic
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: The failed relay has stopped heartbeating and is not forwarding control packets.
agent_observations.agent_1: Two surviving towers can carry emergency load if non-urgent traffic is deprioritized.
agent_observations.agent_2: Broadcasting all traffic on every channel would saturate already noisy storm links.
agent_observations.agent_3: Urgent medical traffic accounts for a small share of total volume but needs predictable latency.
agent_observations.agent_4: Hardware protection thresholds on the surviving towers are well above the projected urgent-only load.

prompt:
A food-delivery control plane sees one district dropping GPS updates and must choose a dispatch policy. Choose the best policy.
A: continue assigning long routes there without adjustment
B: restrict assignments there, use recent known positions carefully, and escalate navigation checks
C: disable ETA messaging globally so customers expect delays everywhere
D: route every courier through one central hub for simpler tracking
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: GPS dropouts are concentrated in one district with recent cell-tower maintenance.
agent_observations.agent_1: Recent last-known positions remain usable for short local handoffs but not for long cross-district routes.
agent_observations.agent_2: ETA messaging failures are localized; the rest of the city remains stable.
agent_observations.agent_3: Escalating navigation health checks in the affected district can be done without touching other districts.
agent_observations.agent_4: Routing everyone through one hub would increase average travel time even where tracking is healthy.

prompt:
A grid-monitoring team receives conflicting outage reports from two substations and one trusted line sensor. Choose the best dispatch target.
A: shut off the full grid segment immediately without confirmation
B: dispatch to the substation consistent with the trusted line sensor and request confirmation from the other
C: ignore the trusted sensor and trust the louder substation alarm
D: wait for public reports before acting
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: The trusted line sensor indicates a fault signature consistent with substation east, not west.
agent_observations.agent_1: West substation recently had a relay maintenance change that increased nuisance alarms.
agent_observations.agent_2: An immediate full shutdown would cut service to two hospitals that show stable voltage now.
agent_observations.agent_3: Field dispatch can verify the east site quickly while a remote confirmation is requested from west.
agent_observations.agent_4: Public reports lag internal telemetry by several minutes and are unreliable during storms.

prompt:
A rescue coordination mesh must allocate its last drone after multiple weak sightings and one medical beacon. Choose the best allocation.
A: send the drone to the medical beacon
B: split the drone mission equally across the weak sightings
C: ignore the beacon because weak sightings cover more total area
D: ground the drone to save battery for tomorrow's operations
Return the single best option.

agent_observations.agent_0: The medical beacon was authenticated recently and maps to a registered rescue wristband.
agent_observations.agent_1: The two weak sightings came from volunteer radio traffic with low position confidence.
agent_observations.agent_2: The drone has enough battery for one high-confidence sortie but not for a broad area search.
agent_observations.agent_3: Weather in the beacon corridor remains flyable for the next twenty minutes only.
agent_observations.agent_4: Ground teams can continue checking the weak-sighting sectors without drone support.
